verses.text: Now concerning spiritual gifts, brethren, I would not have you ignorant.
Ye know that ye were Gentiles, carried away unto these dumb idols, even as ye were led.
Wherefore I give you to understand, that no man speaking by the Spirit of God calleth Jesus accursed: and that no man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost.
Now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit.
And there are differences of administrations, but the same Lord.
And there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God which worketh all in all.
But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal.
For to one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge by the same Spirit;
To another faith by the same Spirit; to another the gifts of healing by the same Spirit;
To another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discerning of spirits; to another divers kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues:
But all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will.
For as the body is one, and hath many members, and all the members of that one body, being many, are one body: so also is Christ.
For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body, whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free; and have been all made to drink into one Spirit.
For the body is not one member, but many.
If the foot shall say, Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body; is it therefore not of the body?
And if the ear shall say, Because I am not the eye, I am not of the body; is it therefore not of the body?
If the whole body were an eye, where were the hearing? If the whole were hearing, where were the smelling?
But now hath God set the members every one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him.
And if they were all one member, where were the body?
But now are they many members, yet but one body.
And the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee: nor again the head to the feet, I have no need of you.
Nay, much more those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary:
And those members of the body, which we think to be less honourable, upon these we bestow more abundant honour; and our uncomely parts have more abundant comeliness.
For our comely parts have no need: but God hath tempered the body together, having given more abundant honour to that part which lacked:
That there should be no schism in the body; but that the members should have the same care one for another.
And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it.
Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular.
And God hath set some in the church, first apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers, after that miracles, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, diversities of tongues.
Are all apostles? are all prophets? are all teachers? are all workers of miracles?
Have all the gifts of healing? do all speak with tongues? do all interpret?
But covet earnestly the best gifts: and yet shew I unto you a more excellent way.

summary: Paul opens a new section with the formula he reserves for contested matters: "Now concerning spiritual gifts, brethren, I would not have you ignorant." He begins by reminding the Corinthians what they were before, "Gentiles, carried away unto these dumb idols, even as ye were led" — a religious past of mute images and unaccountable seizure — and he hands them a first test for any inspired speech: "no man speaking by the Spirit of God calleth Jesus accursed: and that no man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost." Confession, not intensity, marks the Spirit. From that test he lays down the pattern that governs everything after it, a triple refrain that traces variety back to a single source: "there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit," "differences of administrations, but the same Lord," "diversities of operations, but it is the same God which worketh all in all." The purpose clause matters as much as the refrain, since "the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal." A list follows — "the word of wisdom," "the word of knowledge," "faith," "the gifts of healing," "the working of miracles," "prophecy," "discerning of spirits," "divers kinds of tongues," "the interpretation of tongues" — and every item is closed off from boasting by the same clause: all are worked by "that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will." Then comes the image that carries the remainder of the chapter: "For as the body is one, and hath many members, and all the members of that one body, being many, are one body: so also is Christ." Membership is not achieved but conferred, for "by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body, whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free; and have been all made to drink into one Spirit." Paul then works the metaphor from both ends. Against the member who counts himself excluded he sets the foot and the ear: "If the foot shall say, Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body; is it therefore not of the body?" Against the member who counts himself sufficient he sets the eye and the head: "the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee: nor again the head to the feet, I have no need of you." The arrangement belongs to God, for "now hath God set the members every one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him," and that arrangement reverses the ranking men would make, since "those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary" and God has "tempered the body together, having given more abundant honour to that part which lacked." The aim is stated without disguise: "That there should be no schism in the body; but that the members should have the same care one for another," issuing in a shared nervous system where "whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it." The application lands directly on them — "Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular" — and Paul names an ordered arrangement that "God hath set... in the church, first apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers, after that miracles, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, diversities of tongues." A run of questions expecting the answer no — "Are all apostles? are all prophets? are all teachers?... do all speak with tongues? do all interpret?" — forecloses the idea that any one gift is the mark of the Spirit's presence. The chapter ends by permitting ambition and redirecting it: "covet earnestly the best gifts: and yet shew I unto you a more excellent way."
takeaways: The chapter's opening test is doctrinal rather than experiential. Corinth had come out of a world of "dumb idols" whose worshippers were "carried away... even as ye were led," where the mark of the divine was being overtaken by a power that could not speak. Paul refuses to let that be the standard of Christian inspiration and substitutes a confession: "no man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost." The Spirit's signature is articulate and christological, which means an experience is not self-authenticating simply because it is overwhelming, and a plain confession of the lordship of Jesus is already the Spirit's work in a person who has never spoken in tongues.

The threefold refrain — "the same Spirit," "the same Lord," "the same God which worketh all in all" — makes diversity an argument for unity rather than against it. Paul does not flatten the gifts into sameness; he shows that their variety is itself evidence of a single giver, which strips the recipient of any ground for pride, since "all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will." Nothing on the list was earned, chosen, or deserved, so nothing on the list can be a credential.

The purpose clause governs everything: "the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal." A gift is not a possession but an assignment, given to one person for the benefit of others, which reverses the direction Corinth had been reading it in. This is also the standard by which Paul will later rank prophecy above uninterpreted tongues, and it means the question to ask of any spiritual endowment is not what it proves about its bearer but what good it does the assembly.

The body image is aimed at two opposite failures at once. The foot who says "Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body" and the eye who says to the hand "I have no need of thee" commit the same error from opposite ends: both treat their own function as the measure of belonging. Paul's answer to each is the same fact — "now hath God set the members every one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him" — so that self-exclusion and self-sufficiency are both refusals of God's own arrangement.

God's ordering deliberately inverts visible prestige, since "those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary," and God has "tempered the body together, having given more abundant honour to that part which lacked." The stated goal is negative and positive together: "That there should be no schism in the body; but that the members should have the same care one for another." The result is a body with a shared nervous system, where "whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it," so indifference to another Christian's suffering is not merely uncharitable but anatomically impossible for a healthy member.

The closing verses hold two things together that are often set against each other. Structure is divine — "God hath set some in the church, first apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers" — and the ordinal words indicate that the gifts are not interchangeable in value. Yet the questions "Are all apostles? are all prophets?... do all speak with tongues?" rule out any single gift as the universal proof of the Spirit. Ambition is not condemned but reoriented: "covet earnestly the best gifts: and yet shew I unto you a more excellent way," so the chapter that most exalts the charisms ends by subordinating all of them to something else.

crossRefs.label: Romans 12:4-6 — as we have many members in one body, and all members have not the same office
crossRefs.why: Paul makes the same argument to a church he had never visited, and the overlap shows the body image is not an ad hoc rebuke of Corinth but his settled account of the Church. There the practical fruit is stated first — "not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think" — and the gifts are held "according to the grace that is given to us," which supplies the humility that 1 Corinthians 12 argues toward.

crossRefs.label: Ephesians 4:4-16 — There is one body, and one Spirit... he gave some, apostles
crossRefs.why: The unity refrain "one body, and one Spirit... One Lord, one faith, one baptism" restates the triple "same Spirit... same Lord... same God" of this chapter, and the list of those Christ "gave" parallels what "God hath set... in the church." Ephesians adds the goal explicitly — the ministries exist "for the perfecting of the saints" until "the whole body fitly joined together... maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love" — which is the same criterion of profit and edification Paul is applying at Corinth.

crossRefs.label: Acts 2:4-11 — began to speak with other tongues... every man heard them speak in his own language
crossRefs.why: Pentecost supplies the church's founding instance of the gifts Paul is regulating, and the difference is instructive: there the tongues were immediately understood, since "every man heard them speak in his own language," whereas at Corinth an uninterpreted tongue leaves the hearer outside. Reading them together frames the question Paul takes up next, of whether a gift is functioning as sign and communication or only as private experience.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 115:4-8 — They have mouths, but they speak not... They that make them are like unto them
crossRefs.why: Paul's phrase "dumb idols" is not a throwaway insult but a deliberate contrast. The psalm's mockery of images that cannot speak, see, hear, or handle ends with the warning that "they that make them are like unto them," which is exactly the fate Paul says the Corinthians were rescued from when they were "carried away... even as ye were led." The Spirit who now makes them confess "Jesus is the Lord" is the opposite of the speechless gods that once directed them.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 10:16-17 — we being many are one bread, and one body
crossRefs.why: Two chapters earlier Paul had already grounded the oneness of the body in a shared meal: "The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? For we being many are one bread, and one body: for we are all partakers of that one bread." That statement stands behind "by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body... and have been all made to drink into one Spirit," tying the body language to what the church actually does when it gathers rather than to metaphor alone.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 1:10-12 — I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas
crossRefs.why: The letter opened with the very disease this chapter diagnoses anatomically. Paul's plea "that there be no divisions among you" is answered here by God's own design of the body "That there should be no schism in the body," and the party slogans of chapter 1 are the social form of the foot saying "I am not of the body" and the eye saying "I have no need of thee."

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "God hath set some in the church, first apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers" as describing a structure that is divinely instituted rather than merely convenient. The ordinal words are given weight: the arrangement has a real order, with apostolic office at its head, and the verb is that God "hath set" it in place, so the Church's hierarchical constitution is understood as one of the Spirit's works and not a later human overlay on a formless charismatic community. On this reading the hierarchical gifts and the freely distributed charisms come from the same Spirit and are not rivals, the charisms being ordered to the building up of the one body under the pastors who are charged with discerning them. "Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular" is likewise read of a visible, structured communion, since a body with organs, offices, and mutual dependence is precisely not an invisible aggregate.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings emphasize the sovereign and unpredictable distribution stated in the same passage — the Spirit is "dividing to every man severally as he will" — and read the numbered list as ranking usefulness for edification rather than establishing a chain of jurisdiction. Since "the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man," the whole membership is gifted and the body image is taken to support the common priesthood of all believers, with ordered ministry serving the congregation rather than standing over it. Many hold that apostles and prophets belong to the Church's foundation and are unrepeatable, so the ranked list describes the era in which the gospel was first delivered rather than a permanent office structure; others accept enduring offices but derive their shape from Scripture rather than from an unbroken succession. Both traditions affirm that the ordering is God's own, that no member may opt out or declare another unnecessary, and that gifts exist for the body and not for the holder.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic reading, "by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body, whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free; and have been all made to drink into one Spirit" refers to the sacrament actually received. Baptism is not a picture of an incorporation that happens elsewhere; it is the means by which the Spirit joins a person to the visible Body of Christ, which is why the barriers of nation and status are named as abolished in the same breath. The drinking clause is heard alongside the Church's other sacramental life, so that initiation and the shared cup together constitute the one body that Paul then describes organ by organ, and membership in Christ is inseparable from membership in the concrete communion of the Church.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the baptism in view as the Spirit's own act of uniting the believer to Christ, which water baptism signifies and seals rather than accomplishes, and they take the resulting body to be first the whole company of the redeemed rather than a single visible institution. Sacramental Protestants stay close to the Catholic reading in tying sign and thing signified tightly together, while others insist the operative agent in the sentence is the Spirit and the instrument is faith. Pentecostal and charismatic readers add a further distinction, holding that a subsequent baptism in the Holy Spirit empowers for service, while acknowledging that this particular verse describes something universal, since Paul says "we all" without exception. All sides agree that no one joins the body by self-selection, that the divisions of Jew and Gentile, bond and free are dissolved by it, and that the same Spirit is given to every member.
